arm: H5 history-modulated LMR (retest of the arm rejected at 150 ms)
verdict: SHELVED without playing games. Structural no-op, not a tuning failure.
hypothesis: The log-log LMR schedule asks only 'how late is this move'. History answers 'is this move actually good' directly, so shifting the reduction by history should recover Elo. Previously measured +3.5 Elo at 150 ms and rejected on the harness later shown to understate depth-dependent arms ~2.3x, so it was queued for retest at >= 1000 ms.

why_it_was_never_played.rule: CLAUDE.md: matein3 node count plus mates-solved is a ~4 s pre-screen; if a change moves nodes <5% or loses a mate, do not spend games on it.
why_it_was_never_played.measured: Three scale settings produced a byte-identical node count (10011374), and the finest produced 10009642 -- a change of 1,732 nodes out of 10 million, or 0.017%.
why_it_was_never_played.conclusion: Far below the threshold. Playing 400 games would have measured noise.

the_structural_reason.finding: Move ordering ALREADY sorts by history, so the moves with meaningful history land at the front of the list. LMR only fires at idx >= 3. The late-move region LMR can reduce therefore contains almost exclusively moves whose history is near zero -- there is nothing left for history to modulate.
the_structural_reason.consequence: History-modulated LMR is close to a tautological no-op in an engine whose ordering is already history-driven. The only usable signal is the negative tail (moves history actively dislikes), and that tail is thin.
the_structural_reason.this_explains: The original +3.5 Elo at 150 ms. That was almost certainly noise rather than a real-but-small effect, which changes how the arm should be read in the historical record.

measured_history_distribution.method: Instrumented probe: run a real search, then report percentiles of non-zero history_table entries.
measured_history_distribution.why_it_matters: This is the number needed to set any history-scaled constant, and it had never been measured. The distribution is far more skewed than a HIST_MAX-relative scale assumes.
measured_history_distribution.read: HIST_MAX is 16384, but the 90th percentile of touched entries is 4-9. The table is bimodal: a thin tail of strongly-reinforced moves and a large mass at ~0. Any constant expressed as a fraction of HIST_MAX will therefore be a no-op. Scale from this table instead.

what_would_actually_be_needed: A signal ORTHOGONAL to the one already used for ordering. Continuation history (H2) is the obvious candidate: it is indexed by the previous move, so it can disagree with plain history and therefore carries information about moves that ordering has already pushed late. That arm remains untested at >= 1000 ms.

Alternatively, modulate on something the ordering does not consume -- static exchange evaluation of the quiet move, or whether it is a killer/counter -- so the modulator is not measuring the same quantity that placed the move where it is.
Do NOT simply retune the divisor. Four settings spanning 512x produced no tree change; the constant is not the problem.
cost: No games played. The pre-screen and an instrumented probe cost a few minutes and prevented a ~2 hour 400-game screen that would have returned noise.
caveats: The distribution probe is three position/depth samples, not a corpus. The 90th-percentile figure is stable across all three, but the tail values are not well characterised.
The structural argument depends on ordering being history-driven, which is true after H1. It would not hold for an engine that orders quiets some other way.

The arm was shelved on tree-change evidence, not on Elo. It remains formally possible that a change too small to move matein3 nodes by 0.02% is worth Elo in real games -- but that is not a bet the protocol supports funding.
